extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, students and writers interested in culture, literature, and moral-philosophical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or analysing essays about 'culture' that judge literature, education, and social life by broad intellectual and moral standards (e.g., the balance of thinking and doing, humanizing knowledge, social manners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real thought and real beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture must be permeated by 'real thought and real beauty; real sweetness and real light' rather than shallow or spurious substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page insists on authenticity: culture should present 'real thought' and 'real beauty' (not mere affectation). Warnings/anti-patterns: manufactured popular intellectual food or facile sentimentality that only imitates culture's forms. Aim to nourish readers, not to give them ready-made judgments or watchwords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize and diffuse the best knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture 'seeks to do away with classes; to make the best that has been thought and known in the world current everywhere' and to 'humanize' knowledge so it is usable outside cliques of the cultivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: remove harsh, uncouth, difficult, abstract, professional, exclusive aspects of knowledge so it can be effective and understood broadly while remaining 'the best' thought of the time. Example figures praised for this task: Abelard, Lessing, Herder. Aim for accessibility without degrading quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not teach down or indoctrinate the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture 'does not try to teach down to the level of inferior classes' nor 'try to win them for this or that sect... with ready-made judgments and watchwords.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: ordinary popular literature tailored to presumed 'masses' and partisan/religious propaganda that adapts ideas to win followers. Instead of simplifying into slogans, present ideas that 'nourish, and not bind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Men of culture as apostles of equality
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This is the social idea; and the men of culture are the true apostles of equality.' Culture's social aim is to promote equality by spreading humane knowledge and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture's diffusion contributes to social equality by making knowledge, beauty, and manners common currency. Evaluate work by how it promotes mutual understanding, breaks class barriers, and cultivates social empathy rather than reinforcing hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Hellenism (knowing) and Hebraism (doing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two rival but complementary forces—Hellenism (the life of thought: seeing things as they really are, spontaneity of consciousness) and Hebraism (the life of conduct: obedience, strictness of conscience, self-conquest)—should be held in balance; the human spirit needs both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic guidance: identify which tendency a work or society emphasizes. Neither should be absolutized; excellence often requires alternating or integrating both impulses. The ideal cultural stance avoids exclusive preponderance of either knowing or doing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hellenism: clarity of thought, perception, and cultivation of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Hellenism's uppermost idea 'is to see things as they really are' and it pursues 'spontaneity of consciousness', clearness of mind, the enjoyment of beauty—giving 'sweetness and light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating writing, value perceptual acuity, intellectual openness, elegancy of expression, and aesthetic cultivation. Beware of Hellenism's possible moral laxity or insensitivity—its strength is intellectual and aesthetic, not necessarily moral discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebraism: priority of conduct, obedience, and moral discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebraism emphasizes 'conduct and obedience', 'strictness of conscience', self-conquest, and an acute sense of sin; its aim is moral perfection through vigilant practice and devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing work, look for moral seriousness, emphasis on duty and self-discipline, and treatments that awaken conscience. Note Hebraism's propensity to generate prescriptive rules and rigorous ethical demands; this is valuable where formation of character is needed but can become over-rigid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure your 'light be not darkness' (avoid false certainties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted counsel: 'First, never go against the best light you have; secondly, take care that your light be not darkness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution for writers/thinkers: be energetic in following convictions but continually test them to avoid mistaking error for truth. Evaluate claims and rhetoric for self-awareness, humility, and ongoing critical examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate social life and manners to promote equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'power of social life and manners' humanizes people and is 'a promoter of equality' because humane manners make men feel equal and considerate toward one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion: writing or cultural education should encourage humane social behavior (manners, public spirit) as part of humanization. Examples: French 'esprit de société' and Italian popular judgments of beauty. Consider social manners as complementary to intellectual and moral cultivation in promoting equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance humanity along multiple lines (knowledge, conduct, beauty, social life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanization is multi-dimensional: different nations may be preeminent in different elements (knowledge, conduct, beauty, social life); full culture requires progress in all these lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or judging cultural writing, avoid single-axis prescriptions. Good cultural work addresses multiple facets—intellectual, moral, aesthetic, and social—and recognizes contributions from various traditions. Evaluate comprehensiveness and pluralism in the aims of a work.
